passages.t: Eliphaz again: your own mouth condemns you
passages.happening:
‘Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied’ (verse 1). “Does a wise man answer with empty counsel or fill his belly with the hot east wind?” (verse 2). Job's words, he says, undermine the fear of God. “Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you” (verse 6).

“Were you the first man ever born? Were you brought forth before the hills? Do you listen in on the council of God or limit wisdom to yourself?” (verses 7-8). The gray-haired are on the friends' side, men older than Job's father. “Are the consolations of God not enough for you, even words spoken gently to you?” (verse 11).

Then Eliphaz repeats his earlier teaching. “What is man, that he should be pure, or one born of woman, that he should be righteous?” (verse 14). If even the heavens are not pure in God's sight, how much less a man ‘who drinks injustice like water?’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The second round of speeches begins, and the tone hardens. In the first round the friends offered Job a way back: repent and be restored. In the second, running through chapter 21, they offer almost no promise at all. They describe at length the terrible end of the wicked and leave Job to draw the conclusion about himself.

The hot east wind was the scorching wind from the desert that withered crops. Born before the hills would make someone as old as the world itself, and the council of God was the heavenly assembly where his plans are spoken. Eliphaz is saying that Job talks as if he were the first man or one of God's advisers.

There is an irony the reader can see. The reader has already been shown God's council in chapters 1 and 2. None of the speakers were there, Eliphaz included.

Eliphaz calls the friends' words the consolations of God. Job will answer in the next chapter by calling them miserable comforters. And Eliphaz charges Job with undermining the fear of God, a serious charge against a man introduced as one who feared God (1:1).
passages.later: Proverbs uses Eliphaz's phrase for wisdom itself, present at creation: “Before the mountains were settled, before the hills, I was brought forth” (Proverbs 8:25).
passages.asks: Eliphaz called his hard words the consolations of God. Ask whether you have ever named your own opinion as God's comfort. And ask what would change if you listened to a person in pain as if you had not been in God's council either.

passages.t: The fate of the wicked man
passages.happening:
“Listen to me and I will inform you. I will describe what I have seen, what was declared by wise men and was not concealed from their fathers” (verses 17-18).

“A wicked man writhes in pain all his days; only a few years are reserved for the ruthless” (verse 20). Sounds of terror fill his ears, and in his prosperity the destroyer attacks. He is marked for the sword and knows his day of darkness is near. Why? ‘For he has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty’ (verse 25).

His face is fat with ease, but he will live in ruined cities. His wealth will not last. He is like a vine that drops its unripe grapes, an olive that sheds its blossoms. ‘For the company of the godless will be barren, and fire will consume the tents of bribery. They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb is pregnant with deceit’ (verses 34-35).
passages.hearers:
Eliphaz comes from Teman in Edom, a region famous for its wise men, and he presents this portrait as ancestral wisdom, pure and unmixed, handed down in a people undisturbed by outsiders. The oldest teaching, the ancient world believed, was the most reliable.

The portrait moves from the wicked man's inner terror, to its cause, defiance of God, and then to his end in ruin, fire and barrenness. A vine that drops its fruit and an olive that sheds its blossoms were pictures of a life that comes to nothing.

Nothing in the portrait names Job. But everything in it is aimed at him: the destroyer in his prosperity, the fire, the empty tent. Eliphaz does not say Job is the wicked man. He lets Job draw the conclusion.
passages.later: A psalm uses the same picture of sin bearing its own fruit: “Behold, the wicked man travails with evil; he conceives trouble and births falsehood” (Psalm 7:14). And another psalm tells of a faithful man who almost lost his footing when he saw the wicked prosper: “For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (Psalm 73:3).
passages.hard:
Is Eliphaz's portrait of the wicked man true? Do the wicked always live in terror and die in ruin?

Much of it matches what Scripture says elsewhere about the end of those who defy God, and Proverbs often speaks of the wicked coming to ruin. But Eliphaz presents it as a rule anyone can watch at work in this life, and that is where Job pushes back. In chapter 21 Job will answer that many wicked people live long, die in peace and are buried with honor. Psalm 73 records the same troubled observation before its writer understands their final end.

Many readers conclude that Eliphaz's portrait is true of God's final judgment but false as a description of how every life visibly turns out. The book of Job exists in large part to expose that difference. And Eliphaz's use of the portrait against a suffering man is part of what God later rebukes (42:7). No one may hold up a picture of the wicked man's ruin to a person whose life has fallen apart, as if the two were the same.
passages.asks: Eliphaz never said Job was wicked. He described the wicked and let the picture make the charge. Ask whether you have ever accused someone that way, by hinting. And ask whether you could say plainly what you think, or whether you should say nothing at all.
